scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Molly dancing originated in East Anglia as a tradition performed by out-of-work ploughboys during the harsh winter months.
First attested in the 1820s, it became strongly tied to Boxing Day and Plough Monday, a date celebrated in the region since the fifteenth century.
Unemployed farmworkers danced both to entertain themselves and to collect money during a season with little agricultural labor.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Molly dance was tied directly to the midwinter calendar, specifically Boxing Day (26 December) and Plough Monday (the first Monday after Epiphany).
It functioned as both community entertainment and economic survival, offering seasonal income for farmworkers when fields lay dormant.
While pre-revival teams were strictly male, modern revival teams feature mixed-gender participation and perform both in traditional winter runs and at festivals throughout the year.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The traditional Molly dances recorded by collectors were mostly ordinary social dances of the 19th century adapted into simple longways sets.
Rather than light or intricate step patterns, dancers used heavy stepping.
Dancers moved in line or set formations, often led or accompanied by character figures such as a sweeper who cleared a space with a broom.
Watch for Sweeper march, Heavy longways set step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Molly dance was typically provided by a hired musician rather than an agricultural worker.
Fiddlers provided the standard accompaniment until the late nineteenth century, when concertinas and accordions became popular choices.
Listen for the Fiddle, Concertina, Accordion, Percussion.
The pulse is 2/4 or 6/8 at about 110 beats a minute.
A rhythmic, rustic winter sound driven by accordion, concertina, or fiddle playing popular tunes, sometimes supported by basic percussion.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The traditional attire of Molly dancers consisted of ordinary working clothes decorated with rosettes and bright ribbons, topped with top hats or frock coats.
Dancers blackened their faces with soot as a disguise.
A key feature was cross-dressing: at least one man, and in some accounts half the team, wore women's clothing.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Historical collectors Joseph Needham, Arthur Peck, William Palmer, Russell Wortley, and Cyril Papworth documented the few remaining traditional dances in Cambridgeshire villages like Girton, Histon, Comberton, and Little Downham.
In 1976, folk musician Ashley Hutchings raised public awareness of the style through the compilation album Rattlebone and Ploughjack.
The original tradition was concentrated in the East Anglian fenlands, particularly Cambridgeshire.
Derived from 19th-century East Anglian social dances and winter plough rituals, Molly dance is a distinct variant within the broader family of English Morris display dances.

wardrobe.from_sources: The traditional attire of Molly dancers consisted of ordinary working clothes decorated with rosettes and bright ribbons, topped with top hats or frock coats. Dancers blackened their faces with soot as a disguise. A key feature was cross-dressing: at least one man, and in some accounts half the team, wore women's clothing. Teams were accompanied by characters such as an umbrella man to shield the musician from the elements, a broom-bearing sweeper, and a box bearer. Modern revival sides often maintain face paint, masks, ribbons, or cross-dressing while discarding standard Cotswold morris elements like handkerchiefs and leg bells.
